name: Cultural bias
statement: Cultural bias is the error of reading a result obtained in one population as a fact about people, when the population sampled is an unusual one.
meaning: The everyday sense is judging another culture by the standards of one's own. The version that can be measured is narrower and belongs to research practice: a finding is collected in one population and written up as a finding about humans. Henrich, Heine and Norenzayan gave that version its name in 2010. Their abstract says behavioural scientists "routinely publish broad claims about human psychology and behavior in the world's top journals based on samples drawn entirely from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies". Researchers then assume, often implicitly, either that variation across populations is small or that these "standard subjects" are as representative as any other group. Their review covers visual perception, fairness, cooperation, spatial reasoning, categorisation and inferential induction, moral reasoning, reasoning styles, self-concepts and the heritability of IQ. The conclusion is that WEIRD subjects are "frequent outliers" and "among the least representative populations one could find for generalizing about humans". Three claims sit inside the name and come apart under testing. The first is about who gets sampled, which is a counting exercise and is settled; entry 82 carries the journal counts. The second is about whether the sampling matters for any given result, which is an empirical question with a per-effect answer. The third is about measurement, and asks whether a questionnaire means the same thing in every population it is given to. That one is settled scale by scale, and a scale can fail it however wide the sampling.

origin.who: Joseph Henrich, Steven J. Heine and Ara Norenzayan
origin.note: "The weirdest people in the world?", Behavioral and Brain Sciences 33(2-3), 61 to 83. The paper coined the WEIRD acronym and assembled the comparative evidence; it does not claim to have named the general problem, and credits Arnett's 2008 count of journal samples for the sampling figures it quotes.

evidence: The strongest cases in the review are ones where a low-level process was expected to be invariant and was not. Henrich and colleagues report Segall, Campbell and Herskovits's 1966 project on the Müller-Lyer illusion across 16 societies, 14 of them small-scale. The measure is the point of subjective equality, the percentage by which one segment must be lengthened before the two look equal. American undergraduates on average needed the segment about a fifth longer, the extreme of the distribution, and their value differs from every other society studied. The San foragers of the Kalahari showed a value that cannot be distinguished from zero, so the illusion is not an illusion for them. Henrich and colleagues note that many of the other populations cannot be distinguished from one another, and that the same pattern of population-level variation appeared for the Sander-Parallelogram and both Horizontal-Vertical illusions. Their second case is bargaining behaviour. Figure 3 of the paper reports dictator and ultimatum games run in 15 societies. The United States adult non-student sample has the highest mean dictator offer, nearly double that of the Hadza of Tanzania and the Tsimane of the Bolivian Amazon. In the ultimatum game the United States has the second highest mean offer, behind the Sursurunga of Papua New Guinea. On the punishment side, the income-maximising offer for the United States is tied with the Sursurunga and is five times higher than for 70% of the other societies. The authors' summary is that people from industrialised societies "consistently occupy the extreme end of the human distribution". A different kind of evidence concerns what authors then say about their samples. Rad, Martingano and Ginges coded every empirical article in Psychological Science for 2014, 223 original research articles yielding 428 studies and 450 samples. Fifty-one studies, 11.41%, gave no information from which the country or region could be coded. Of the remainder, 57.76% drew on samples from the United States and 94.15% sampled Western countries, counting English-speaking countries, Europe and Israel. Their harder finding is about bounding. Over 72% of abstracts carried no information about the population sampled, and 83% of studies reported no analysis of any effect of their sample's diversity. Over 85% did not discuss possible effects of culture and context on the findings, and 84% did not recommend studying the phenomenon in other cultures. Muthukrishna and colleagues put a number on the distances involved. They applied the fixation index from population genetics to the World Values Survey, treating questions as loci and answers as alleles, and built a scale of cultural distance from the United States. Japan and Norway come out similarly distant from the United States, at .115 and .124. Comparing survey regions inside the four largest populations, India has the largest mean regional diversity at .11, the European Union .09, China .05, and the United States .01. Measurement is the third strand and carries its own evidence. Davidov tested the 21-item human values instrument in the second round of the European Social Survey. Multi-group confirmatory factor analysis across 25 countries did not support configural invariance. In 11 of them at least one further pair of values had to be combined, leaving fewer than seven values. Cutting the set to 14 countries gave configural invariance with seven values, at CFI .914 and RMSEA .013, and metric invariance held at CFI .903 and RMSEA .014. Scalar invariance, the condition for comparing national means, was rejected at CFI .794 and RMSEA .019. Davidov concludes that value means may not be compared across those 14 countries. That is bias in the instrument rather than in the sample, and a wider sample does not cure it.

replication.headline: Cross-population variation is large in the domains Henrich and colleagues reviewed. Many Labs 2 found WEIRDness moderating three of 28 effects, on a test later estimated to have at most 28% power.
replication.detail: Many Labs 2 is the direct test, because it ran the same 28 preregistered protocols across many countries and then asked whether WEIRDness moderated any of them. The published abstract states that "exploratory comparisons revealed little heterogeneity between Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic (WEIRD) cultures and less WEIRD cultures". The accepted manuscript gives the working. Samples were scored on a WEIRDness index built from country rankings and split at the mean. Slate 1 held 42 WEIRD samples against 22 less WEIRD ones, and Slate 2 held 44 against 17. For 13 of the 14 effects that were reliable and in the same direction as the original, the finding appeared in both WEIRD and less WEIRD samples "with similar effect magnitudes". The single exception was Huang, Tse and Cho's cardinal direction and socioeconomic status effect, where the less WEIRD samples showed no overall effect and wide variability. After correcting for multiple comparisons, three of the 28 effects showed evidence of moderation by WEIRDness: Huang and colleagues, Knobe's side-effect effect, entry 15, and Norenzayan and colleagues on formal versus intuitive reasoning. For Norenzayan, the cultural difference ran opposite to the original result. The project's own summary is that variability in observed effect sizes "was attributable more to the effect being studied than to the sample or setting in which it was studied". Schimmelpfennig and colleagues, a group that includes all three authors of the 2010 review, re-examined that exploratory analysis in 2024. Their simulations put the power of the WEIRDness moderation test between 0 and 28%, depending on how much cultural influence was simulated. Where an effect was modelled to vanish entirely in countries unlike the United States, power across the project's chosen criteria ran from 6% to 44%. They also report that the samples barely leave the WEIRD range. Mean cultural distance from the United States was .055 taking sample sites as the unit and .062 taking participants, against .069 between the United States and Germany. Ninety-one per cent of samples scored below .15 on that index, where world distances from the United States reach about .3. Their preregistered re-analysis swapped the WEIRDness split for that continuous distance. It raised effect sizes for most effects and only marginally increased the number reaching significance, so it did not overturn the Many Labs 2 conclusion. That is the finding that pulls against the review, and neither displaces the other. No single effect size stands for cultural bias, so the structured fields are left empty and the numbers stay per-effect.

study.cite: Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490.

limits: Many Labs 2 sets out its own limits and they are the main ones here. The authors write that their approach "characterized cultural differences at the most general level possible", a dichotomy of WEIRDness, and "ignored the rich diversity within that categorization". The distribution is skewed. Their discussion says samples scoring above 0.70 were classed WEIRD, where the method section describes a split at the observed mean. On either reading the WEIRD samples are alike in WEIRDness and the less WEIRD samples vary widely among themselves. They add that a true examination "would need to more deliberately vary sampling across all dimensions" of the acronym. The analysis also does not address regional variation, such as the difference between American and British samples. Their sampling was wide in countries and narrow in kind, with 39 United States samples and 86 samples from 35 other countries and territories. None of the 28 effects was picked for being culture-sensitive, so the test asks whether WEIRDness moderates a slate of mostly Western social and cognitive findings, not whether the domains Henrich and colleagues reviewed vary. The two bodies of evidence also differ in what they sample: Segall's project and the small-scale-society economic games reached foragers, horticulturalists and pastoralists, and Many Labs 2 recruited through universities and online panels. The power critique has its own limit. Schimmelpfennig and colleagues say plainly that any re-analysis of the Many Labs 2 data, including theirs, is constrained by the same lack of power. Their evidence is that the design could not have found moderation, not that moderation is there. The measurement strand is narrower still. Davidov tested one 21-item instrument in one survey round, so his result bounds the European Social Survey value scale and not questionnaires in general. Provenance is uneven. The Segall figures and the 15-society bargaining results are read off Henrich and colleagues' review. Segall's 1966 book was not obtained. Cambridge served a landing page for Henrich et al. (2005) on 21 September 2026, and no route to a PDF was found. Those bargaining figures are Phase II results, which the review attributes to Henrich and colleagues' 2010 paper in Science, so the 2005 paper is not their source. The Many Labs 2 copy at the publisher met a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, under three user agents, which answers HTTP 403 rather than asking for payment. The text quoted here comes from the accepted manuscript in LSE Research Online, and the published abstract from the OpenAlex record for the DOI. The two agree on every figure used above. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Europe PMC and the open web on 21 September 2026 found no second multi-site project that tested WEIRDness as a moderator across a comparable slate of effects.
misreadings: The first error is treating an unrepresentative sample as a refuted result. A sample that is unusual makes a claim about humans unsafe, and it does not make the claim false, which is why the question has to be settled effect by effect. Many Labs 2 settled it for 28 of them and mostly found no cultural moderation. The second error is reading less WEIRD as East Asian. Muthukrishna and colleagues note that the most commonly studied non-Western nations, Japan, Hong Kong and China, are nowhere near the extreme of their American scale. Japan sits about as far from the United States as Norway does. The third error is treating WEIRD as a synonym for Western. It names five dimensions, and the one large test of it collapsed them into a single country-level score, as its authors say in as many words. The fourth error is thinking a demographically varied American sample answers the objection. On the cultural fixation index the United States has the least regional diversity of the four large populations Muthukrishna and colleagues compare, .01 against India's .11. The fifth error is reading the Many Labs 2 null as a demonstration that culture does not moderate psychological effects. Schimmelpfennig and colleagues searched the citing literature and found over 50 articles invoking the paper for the moderating role of culture or for WEIRD sampling. A test with at most 28% power returns a null whether or not the thing is there. The sixth error is treating the measurement question as the sampling question. An instrument can fail scalar invariance across countries that are each sampled well, and then country means cannot be compared however the participants were recruited. The seventh error is confusing this entry with the counting exercise. How WEIRD the published literature is, and whether that has changed, is a question about journal samples and belongs to selection bias at entry 82.

sources.text: Henrich, J., Heine, S. J., & Norenzayan, A. (2010). The weirdest people in the world? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 33(2-3), 61-83. Full text read from the authors' PDF at the University of British Columbia, which carries the target article together with the commentaries. That PDF is the pre-pagination copy, numbered 1 to 75; the page range 61 to 83 comes from the Crossref record for the DOI, read on 21 September 2026. The Müller-Lyer figures are Henrich and colleagues reporting Segall, Campbell and Herskovits (1966). The bargaining figures are their description of their own Figure 3, which its caption marks as Phase II and which the text attributes to Henrich et al. (2010).

Klein, R. A., Vianello, M., Hasselman, F., et al. (2018). Many Labs 2: Investigating variation in replicability across samples and settings. Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(4), 443-490. The publisher's copy met a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026 under three user agents, answering HTTP 403. The version of record was read in full that day in the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam repository, and it is the source of the figures here. Its abstract says eight effects had a tau near or slightly above .10, where the accepted manuscript in LSE Research Online says nine; nothing quoted here depends on that count. The article says there were 125 samples, of which 15 sites ran both slates, so 125 is a count of samples and not of laboratories.

Rad, M. S., Martingano, A. J., & Ginges, J. (2018). Toward a psychology of Homo sapiens: Making psychological science more representative of the human population. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 115(45), 11401-11405. The PubMed Central page answered curl with a reCAPTCHA under three user agents on 21 September 2026, and the Europe PMC XML route returned HTTP 500, so the text was read through the fetching tool rather than saved as a file. Every figure quoted above was taken back as a verbatim sentence.

Full text read from the Europe PMC fullTextXML route for PMC7357184, after the rendered PubMed Central page answered with a reCAPTCHA on 21 September 2026.

Jones, B. C., DeBruine, L. M., Flake, J. K., et al. (2021). To which world regions does the valence-dominance model of social perception apply? Nature Human Behaviour, 5(1), 159-169. Author manuscript read at Strathprints; the page range comes from the Crossref record for the DOI. Its abstract records 11 world regions, 41 countries and 11,570 participants, and reports that the model generalised across regions under the original analysis strategy and generalised much less under a method allowing correlated dimensions. Cited as a second cross-regional test rather than for any figure above.

Schimmelpfennig, R., Spicer, R., White, C. J. M., Gervais, W., Norenzayan, A., Heine, S., Henrich, J., & Muthukrishna, M. (2024). Full text read from the Europe PMC fullTextXML route for PMC11461273, after the rendered PubMed Central page answered with a reCAPTCHA. The power figures, the cultural distance figures and the citation count are this paper's own.

Full text read from the journal's own PDF at the University of Konstanz. Cited for the measurement strand only.
